'''''Carduus nutans''''' is a [[biennial plant]] in the daisy and sunflower family [[Asteraceae]] with the common names '''musk thistle''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''nodding thistle''', and '''nodding plumeless thistle'''. It is native to regions of Europe, Central Asia, and North Africa, where it is a scattered pasture plant.<ref name="Jongejans-2008">{{Cite journal |last1=Jongejans |first1=Eelke |last2=Shea |first2=Katriona |last3=Skarpaas |first3=Olav |last4=Kelly |first4=Dave |last5=Sheppard |first5=Andy W. |last6=Woodburn |first6=Tim L. |date=2008 |title=Dispersal and demography contributions to population spread of ''Carduus nutans'' in its native and invaded ranges |url=https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2745.2008.01367.x |journal=Journal of Ecology |language=en |volume=96 |issue=4 |pages=687–697 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2745.2008.01367.x |bibcode=2008JEcol..96..687J |issn=0022-0477|hdl=2066/65635 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="CSIRO-2012">{{Cite book |title=Biological control of weeds in Australia |date=2012 |publisher=CSIRO Publishing |isbn=978-0-643-09993-7 |editor-last=Julien |editor-first=M. H. |location=Collingwood, Vic |oclc=770639865 |editor-last2=McFadyen |editor-first2=R. E. |editor-last3=Cullen |editor-first3=Jim}}</ref><ref name="Gassmann-2002">{{Cite journal |last1=Gassmann |first1=A. |last2=Kok |first2=L.-T. |date=2002 |title=Musk Thistle (Nodding Thistle) |journal=USDA Forest Service Publication FHTET-2002-04 |page=413}}</ref> The musk thistle has been declared as invasive in North America, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa.<ref name="CSIRO-2012" />

==Description==
''Carduus nutans'' is a [[Monocarpy|monocarpic]] herb and is classified as a biennial thistle, though it can have varying phenology depending on climate and habitat.<ref name="Young-2017">{{Cite journal |last1=Young |first1=Stephen L. |last2=Clements |first2=David R. |last3=DiTommaso |first3=Antonio |date=2017 |title=Climate Dynamics, Invader Fitness, and Ecosystem Resistance in an Invasion-Factor Framework |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/invasive-plant-science-and-management/article/climate-dynamics-invader-fitness-and-ecosystem-resistance-in-an-invasionfactor-framework/91B976F606814B4CAF35628B20323F4F |journal=Invasive Plant Science and Management |language=en |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=215–231 |doi=10.1017/inp.2017.28 |bibcode=2017IPSM...10..215Y |issn=1939-7291|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Mature plants can reach {{convert|2.7|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} in height with multi-branched stems. The leaves are prickly and jagged and can reach up to {{Convert|40|cm|ft|abbr=on}} in length.<ref name="Spellenberg-2012">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/362/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |pages=362–363 |orig-date=1979}}</ref> The leaves are dark green, coarsely [[Bipinnate|bipinnately]] lobed, with a smooth, waxy surface and sharp yellow-brown to whitish [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|spines]] at the tips of the lobes. They are more or less hairy on top, and wooly on the veins below.<ref name="The Wild Flower Key2">{{cite book |last=Rose |first=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |publisher=Frederick Warne & Co |year=1981 |isbn=0-7232-2419-6 |pages=382–383 |author-link=Francis Rose}}</ref> The stem is cottony/hairy, <small><big>with thin ribs along them.</big><ref name="Spellenberg-2012" /></small> The plants develop a [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]], with large leaves up to about {{convert|40|cm|abbr=off}} long.<ref name="Spellenberg-2012" /> The seeds are able to germinate between {{Convert|15 and 30|C|}}, thriving in conditions that offer moist soil and an alternating day/night temperature.<ref name="Han-2013">{{Cite journal |last1=Han |first1=Chengchou |last2=Young |first2=Stephen L. |date=2013 |title=Ecology of Musk Thistle (''Carduus nutans'') Seed Germination for Grasslands of Temperate Climates |journal=Weed Science |volume=61 |issue=4 |pages=549–556 |doi=10.1614/ws-d-13-00015.1 |bibcode=2013WeedS..61..549H |issn=0043-1745}}</ref> A single plant is able to produce around 100 seeds per flower, up to about 20,000 seeds per plant.<ref name="Han-2013" /> Seeds are mainly wind dispersed<ref name="Young-2017" /> and can survive in the soil seed bank for up to 20 years.<ref name="Jongejans-2006">{{Cite journal |last1=JONGEJANS |first1=EELKE |last2=SHEPPARD |first2=ANDY W. |last3=SHEA |first3=KATRIONA |date=2006-08-23 |title=What controls the population dynamics of the invasive thistle ''Carduus nutans'' in its native range? |journal=Journal of Applied Ecology |volume=43 |issue=5 |pages=877–886 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2664.2006.01228.x |bibcode=2006JApEc..43..877J |issn=0021-8901}}</ref><ref name="CSIRO-2012"/>

===Flowers===
[[Image:Carduus nutans 180807.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Flower head]] 
[[Image:Carduus nutans habitus.jpeg|thumb|Blooming in grassland habitat]]

The plant bears showy flowers that range from a deep rose to violet color, rarely white.<ref name="Gassmann-2002"/> The large globose [[Inflorescence|flower heads]], containing hundreds of tiny individual flowers, are {{Convert|3–5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}}, rarely to {{cvt|7|cm|frac=4}}, in diameter and occur at the tips of stems. The flower heads commonly droop to a 90° to 120° angle from the stem when mature, hence its alternate name of "nodding thistle". Each plant may produce thousands of straw-colored seeds adorned with plume-like [[Awn (botany)|bristles]]. They are {{cvt|4 to 6|cm|frac=4}} across, with purple-red [[Bract|bracts]].

The number of flower heads per plant is site-dependent and ranges from about 20–50 on good sites and 1–20 on poor sites. Flowering occurs from June to October,<ref name="Spellenberg-2012"/> and seed dissemination occurs approximately one month after the flowers form.

==Distribution and habitat==
''Carduus nutans'' is native to Europe, Western Siberia, Asia, and North Africa.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Rui |last2=Shea |first2=Katriona |date=2012 |title=Integrating multiple disturbance aspects: management of an invasive thistle, ''Carduus nutans'' |journal=Annals of Botany |language=en |volume=110 |issue=7 |pages=1395–1401 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcr312 |issn=1095-8290 |pmc=3489138 |pmid=22199031}}</ref> It has become invasive in North America, Australia, New Zealand, and Southern Africa.<ref name="Jongejans-2006" /> It is abundant in the North American [[Rocky Mountains]].<ref name="Spellenberg-2012" /> The plant can grow at least to an elevation of {{Convert|1830|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lackschewitz |first=Klaus. |title=Vascular plants of west-central Montana: identification guide book / |date=1991 |publisher=U.S. Dept. of Agriculture, Forest Service, Intermountain Research Station |location=Ogden, UT |page=143|doi=10.5962/bhl.title.99925 }}</ref><ref name="Gassmann-2002"/> It typically grows in meadows and [[Grassland|grasslands]], in heavily grazed land in areas such as pastures, and on open disturbed soil such as roadsides and building sites.<ref name="Spellenberg-2012" /> It is found in neutral to [[Acidic soil|acidic soils]]. It spreads rapidly in areas subjected to frequent natural disturbances such as landslides and flooding, but does not grow well in excessively wet, dry, or shady conditions.

==Uses==

===Medicinal===
Herbal decoctions have historically included ''Carduus nutans.'' Turkish folk medicine has used parts of the flowering branches to treat prostate disease.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tuzlaci |first=Ertan |date=2010-01-01 |title=Turkish folk medicinal plants, VIII: Lalapasa (Edirne) |url=http://www.marmaraeczacilikdergisi.com/pdf/pdf_MPJ_241.pdf |journal=Marmara Pharmaceutical Journal |language=en |volume=1 |issue=14 |pages=47–52 |doi=10.12991/201014463 |doi-broken-date=20 October 2025 |issn=1309-0801}}</ref> It has also been documented that it has been used for treatment of liver disease, malaria, constipation, and kidney stones.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kozyra |first1=Małgorzata |last2=Kukula-Koch |first2=Wirginia |last3=Szymański |first3=Michał |date=2022 |title=Phenolic Composition of Inflorescences of ''Carduus nutans'' L. |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cbdv.202100827 |journal=Chemistry & Biodiversity |language=en |volume=19 |issue=3 |article-number=e202100827 |doi=10.1002/cbdv.202100827 |pmid=34964548 |issn=1612-1872|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Ecology==
Climate and habitat play a large role in phenology of ''Carduus nutans''. Classified as a biennial, it can also act as a summer or winter annual, as well as a perennial, depending on varying environmental conditions.<ref name="Han-2013" />

==Invasive species==
''Carduus nutans'' is an [[invasive species]] in various regions around the world, including in disturbed and agricultural settings, pastures, rangelands, along roadsides, and in natural [[Habitat|habitats]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Morocco's Fascinating Flora |url=https://www.morocco.com/blog/morocco-s-fascinating-flora/ |access-date=2020-05-28 |website=Morocco.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Gassmann-2002"/> The first report of ''C. nutans'' in the United States was in Pennsylvania in 1852.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stuckey |first1=Ronald L. |last2=Forsyth |first2=Jane L. |date=January 1971 |title=DISTRIBUTION OF NATURALIZED CARDUUS NUTANS (COMPOSITAE) MAPPED IN RELATION TO GEOLOGY IN NORTHWESTERN OHIO |url=https://kb.osu.edu/bitstream/handle/1811/5585/1/V71N01_001.pdf |journal=The Ohio Journal of Science |volume=71 |issue=1 |pages=1–15 |via=Knowledge Bank, University Libraries}}</ref> It is declared a [[noxious weed]] in many [[U.S. states]], [[Canadian province|Canadian provinces]], [[South Africa]], [[New Zealand]], and [[Australia]].<ref>[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=canu4 USDA] . accessed 4.8.2013</ref> The plant is especially fertile, producing up to 20,000 seeds per plant,<ref name="Han-2013" /> that allows it to take root quickly and replace natural vegetation.<ref name="Gassmann-2002" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Groenteman |first1=R |last2=Kelly |first2=D |last3=Fowler |first3=Sv |last4=Bourdôt |first4=Gw |date=2011 |title=Abundance, phenology and impact of biocontrol agents on nodding thistle ( ''Carduus nutans'' ) in Canterbury 35 years into a biocontrol programme |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00288233.2010.531743 |journal=New Zealand Journal of Agricultural Research |language=en |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=1–13 |doi=10.1080/00288233.2010.531743 |bibcode=2011NZJAR..54....1G |issn=0028-8233}}</ref> Pastures and rangelands suffer from decreased productivity and the sharp spines of the plant make an unsuitable grazing area for livestock.<ref name="Gassmann-2002" /><ref name="Han-2013" />

===Biological control===
Several biological control agents have been released in attempt to control ''C. nutans.'' In Australia, some of those that have been released include ''[[Rhinocyllus conicus]], [[Urophora solstitialis]],'' and ''[[Trichosirocalus horridus]].''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cullen |first=Jim |title=Biological Control of Weeds in Australia |publisher=CSIRO Publishing |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-643-09993-7 |location=Collingwood, Vic. |pages=118–128}}</ref> In the United States there has been success with ''[[Rhinocyllus conicus]], [[Trichosirocalus horridus]], and Puccinia carduorum.''<ref name="Gassmann-2002" /> Previous populations in [[Southern California]] were eradicated, but it remains in northern [[California]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carduus nutans (Musk Thistle) Profile – California Invasive Plant Council |url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/profile/carduus-nutans-profile/}}</ref> When biological control is successful, natural plants are shown to return to the habitat.<ref name="Gassmann-2002" />

==Effects on biodiversity==
''Carduus nutans'' reduces forage biomass availability for livestock through competition for nutrients.<ref name="Han-2013" /> The spiny plants affect movement of animals through the area, further decreasing availability of forage biomass.<ref name="Han-2013" /> It also causes soil erosion on roadways and wastelands.
